items.description: Why I'm buying into uncertainty, watching emerging markets, and not waiting for the floor
items.content:
Last week the stock market posted its first weekly gain in six weeks. The S&P rose 3.4%, the Nasdaq 4.4%. A relief rally — real, and welcome. But the rally is happening inside a structural regime change, not at the end of one, and that distinction will determine everything that matters over the next twelve months.

My honest read: this is one of the more genuinely exciting entry environments I have seen. Not because the macro is clean — it is not — but because historically mispriced assets in genuinely uncertain environments are where long-run returns are made. I am not trying to time the floor exactly. Nobody does that reliably — not retail investors, not the largest asset managers, not the best hedge funds. What they do, and what I think is worth doing now, is position near the floor with high-conviction names and hold the thesis with discipline. That is the approach here.

One other thing worth saying upfront: most macro analysis right now is US-centric to a fault. Emerging markets deserve a serious, open-minded look — the dollar is near a near-term peak, the China AI cycle is running independently of US policy, and EM valuations have not been re-rated anywhere near US levels over the past decade. We will build that out explicitly in coming weeks. This note begins to flag it.

What we are living through in 2026 is not a repeat of April 2025, when Liberation Day tariffs triggered a sharp sell-off that resolved in 22% gains over nine months once policy reversed.1 That episode was a single shock in a healthy macro environment. Today the situation is three shocks simultaneously — each structural in its own right, each interacting with the others in ways that make the macro environment qualitatively harder to navigate than anything since 2008.

The three shocks

  1. Geopolitics — Iran and the Strait of Hormuz

    1. On February 28, US and Israeli forces struck Iran, killing Supreme Leader Khamenei. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz effective March 2 — through which 20 million barrels transit daily, roughly 20% of global seaborne energy supply.2 Shipping traffic has fallen 90–95% from normal levels. As of this morning, Trump has set a Tuesday 8PM ET deadline: reopen or face strikes on power plants and bridges. A 45-day ceasefire framework is being discussed through Pakistan, Egypt, and Turkey as mediators, but has not been agreed.3

    2. WTI is at $111/barrel — up roughly 90% since the conflict began. US gasoline hit $4.11/gallon last week, the highest since 2022.4 Kuwait and Bahrain have had petrochemical facilities struck by Iranian drones in the past 48 hours.5

    3. The point most market commentary misses: this is not a sanctions regime or a tariff that can be unwound by executive order. Reopening the Strait requires a negotiated military settlement between parties that have just killed each other’s leadership. That takes months at minimum, not days — and every week it stays closed, the energy price transmission into core inflation deepens and becomes harder to reverse even after resolution.

  2. Trade — Tariffs at 80-year highs

    1. The US average effective tariff rate stands at 11.0% — the highest since 1943, excluding 2025.6 The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, but Trump immediately invoked Section 122 to impose a 10% global tariff valid for 150 days. Sector tariffs on steel (50%), autos (25%), and semiconductors (25%) remain under separate authority.7 Yale Budget Lab estimates the current regime costs US households $1,230–$1,500 annually in 2026.6 Goldman Sachs confirmed that US companies and consumers absorbed 82% of tariff costs in 2025 — the inverse of what the administration projected.8

    2. The implication most investors are still underweighting: the tariff regime is no longer a negotiating posture that can be reversed by a phone call. It was struck down by the Supreme Court and reconstituted within days under different legal authority with Congressional support. That is not a threat — it is settled policy architecture. Supply chains that reprice to absorb 11% average tariffs do not un-reprice when the political winds shift. The cost is structural and the margin compression is permanent until pricing power recovers, which at current consumer balance sheet conditions is not guaranteed.

  3. Inflation — Structural, with no policy room

    1. US PCE inflation is estimated at 2.7% in 2026 — above the Fed’s 2% target. Core CPI printed 2.4% in February.9 The Fed funds rate is 3.50%, with the dot plot projecting just one cut in all of 2026. Kevin Warsh, who replaced Jerome Powell in January, has signalled tighter-for-longer — and markets are beginning to price a potential hike after June if April and May CPI reflect the full transmission of $110+ crude.10 The March jobs report released Friday was unexpectedly strong at 178K versus 60K forecast, unemployment falling to 4.3%.11

    2. Robust employment eliminates political pressure for emergency cuts and leaves the Fed in the classic stagflation trap: inflation above target, tightening financial conditions, and deteriorating growth outlook — simultaneously.

    3. What makes this shock different from 2022 is that the Fed then had room to act aggressively from near-zero rates. Today it is cutting from 3.50% into an oil shock with a contested leadership transition. The policy toolkit is not just constrained — it is politically complicated in ways that widen the distribution of outcomes and make the rate path genuinely unpredictable for the first time since the post-GFC era.

Why this is structural, not cyclical

In April 2025, when Liberation Day tariffs hit, markets fell nearly 20% in seven weeks and then rallied 32% from the April 8 low. By June 2025, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at all-time highs.1 That rapid recovery was correct — the shock was policy-driven and therefore reversible. Trump paused the tariffs, negotiations began, and the fundamental economic picture had not changed.

The current environment is different because all three shocks are simultaneously live and none can be resolved by a single announcement. The Iran conflict is a military war requiring negotiated ceasefires, not market-sensitive tweets. The tariff regime has been reconstituted through different authority after the Supreme Court ruling, with Congressional support that did not exist in 2025. Inflation above target with oil at $111 can only be resolved by time, lower energy prices, or demand destruction — not by monetary policy that is already constrained.

The risk the market keeps underestimating is not volatility week to week. It is the habit of pricing each shock in isolation, when the three together are doing something different: changing the baseline cost of capital, the cost of energy, and the credibility of the institutions that are supposed to manage both.

The consumer is splitting

One structural feature of the current environment receiving less attention than the geopolitical headlines is the bifurcation of the US consumer. The divergence between upper and lower income households has become measurable, significant, and directly relevant to where equity returns will and will not come from.

Headline consumer data still looks resilient — retail sales rose 0.6% in February 2026 and 3.7% year-over-year. The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index ticked up to 91.8 in March.16 But these aggregates are being driven almost entirely by upper-income households whose financial and real assets have protected purchasing power. The University of Michigan’s March survey found lower-income and non-investing households cautious, with sentiment slipping across every spending category except fitness and childcare.16

When $4.11/gallon gasoline absorbs a disproportionately large share of a fixed monthly income, discretionary spending contracts in ways that aggregate data conceals. Consumer-facing businesses targeting middle-income households should be priced with that risk premium clearly embedded. Many are not.

The pattern that repeats

Before analysing scenarios, we review the one invariant in the history of modern equity markets: every major drawdown has recovered to a new all-time high without exception. Past performance is not an indicator of future returns. This is not a prediction — it is the most robust empirical observation across 150 years of market data.

The S&P 500 10-year annualised return is 10.48% through all of these crises combined. Of the 40 weekly S&P declines of 5%+ since 1980, the following week produced a gain 62% of the time. The worst-feeling moments have historically preceded the strongest recoveries.17 The 2026 YTD decline is modest relative to historical drawdowns — which does not mean it cannot worsen, but it does mean the market is not yet pricing a true crisis.

The three scenarios

We frame three scenarios anchored on the two binary outcomes that will determine the next 90 days: whether the Strait of Hormuz reopens and on what timeline, and whether tariff policy stabilises or escalates further. We weight the resolution scenario at 25% — down from earlier in the week — after Iran formally rejected the temporary ceasefire proposal this morning, leaving the Tuesday deadline as the live hinge point.

China — the second AI arms race

Almost every macro analysis of the current environment focuses on the US-Iran conflict and US tariff policy. Significantly less attention is paid to what China’s technology sector is doing in parallel — and it is directly relevant for capital flows, AI infrastructure demand, and for understanding whether the current sell-off in US technology is the market correctly pricing a structural risk or the market incorrectly applying a domestic policy discount to a global secular trend.

China’s AI-related investment reached approximately $125 billion in 2025, growing 48% year-over-year, with approximately 57% funded directly or indirectly through government mechanisms including subsidies, special-purpose bonds, and designated computing hub incentives.18 ByteDance has committed RMB 160 billion (~$23 billion) in 2026 CapEx, with roughly $13 billion directed to AI processors.19 Alibaba has pledged RMB 380 billion (~$53 billion) over three years for AI and cloud infrastructure, with the CEO indicating the figure will be revised upward.20

The investment implication is specific. Unlike US hyperscalers — whose CapEx has been met with multiple compression and stock prices down 9–21% YTD — Chinese technology names have not faced the same valuation penalty for their infrastructure commitments. The market is not applying the same ROI timeline pressure to ByteDance or Alibaba that it applies to AWS or Google Cloud. This asymmetry is instructive: the global AI infrastructure buildout is accelerating on both sides of the Pacific simultaneously, but the valuation discount is being applied almost entirely to the US side. The China data confirms that the infrastructure supercycle is geopolitically mandated and structurally durable — not a single country’s policy choice that can be reversed by a CFO statement.

More broadly, this is one reason we are watching emerging markets more actively than the consensus currently does. A dollar near its near-term peak, an AI investment cycle running independently in Asia, and EM valuations that have not been re-rated anywhere near US levels over the past decade — that combination is worth dedicated research time. We will build out an explicit EM framework in the coming weeks.

The dollar — a signal worth watching

The US Dollar Index has risen above 100 for the first time since May 2025, touching 100.2 this morning before pulling back slightly on ceasefire reports.21 The near-term case for dollar strength is straightforward: safe-haven demand from the Iran conflict, oil priced in dollars creating mechanical demand from energy importers, and a Fed on hold at 3.50% while the ECB and Bank of Japan face their own pressures.

What makes the current dollar level analytically interesting is its tension with the underlying fiscal picture. The US is running a $1.9 trillion federal deficit in 2026, a condition that historically produces dollar weakness as foreign investors demand higher term premiums to hold Treasury debt. The dollar is simultaneously supported by geopolitical safe-haven flows and undermined by fiscal dynamics that have not changed. The bear case for the dollar is not a prediction — it is a mean reversion trade conditional on conflict resolution. Most institutional forecasts place the DXY in the low-to-mid 90s by December 2026.21 If that materialises, dollar-denominated assets purchased today at a war-risk premium will look different in non-dollar terms. That is a tail risk worth sizing explicitly, not discarding.

The Fed’s political problem

The Federal Reserve faces an institutional dilemma that goes beyond the standard inflation versus growth tradeoff. Kevin Warsh — nominated by Trump in January to replace Jerome Powell, with a Senate Banking Committee confirmation hearing now scheduled for April 16 — presents a genuinely ambiguous policy signal.10 His public record through 2025 emphasised balance sheet reduction and hawkishness on inflation, but markets are currently pricing him as marginally more accommodative than Powell — the logic being that political alignment with an administration demanding cuts will eventually override his stated instincts. That reading may be right, but it is also self-serving for equity bulls and worth questioning. What is not in dispute is the confirmation risk: Senator Thom Tillis has vowed to vote against all Fed nominees until the DOJ drops its criminal probe into Powell, which — given the tight committee arithmetic — could block Warsh from taking office before Powell’s term expires on May 15. That institutional gap is not priced.

Trump, simultaneously, is publicly demanding rate cuts to support growth and ease the political cost of high gasoline prices — creating a collision between political pressure, an unconfirmed nominee whose stance is debated, and an oil shock that argues for the opposite of accommodation. The risk is not that the Fed loses formal independence — it is that the uncertainty premium markets apply to the rate path widens materially as three different versions of Fed policy are simultaneously in play: Powell’s current hold, Warsh’s ambiguous signal, and Trump’s public demands. When the expected path of rates is institutionally contested across all three dimensions at once, markets price a wider distribution of outcomes. That shows up in higher equity volatility and multiple compression that precedes any actual earnings deterioration. It is arguably the most underpriced macro risk in the current environment.

Valuation — all major technology at or below historical mean P/E

Against this macro backdrop, every major technology name we track is trading at or below its 10-year historical mean P/E. The compression is regime-driven and largely uniform — the market is applying the same discount to contracted infrastructure revenue as it is to speculative CapEx, which seems like a mistake worth acting on.

Position deep-dive · Coming this week

Oracle — why $553B of contracted backlog changes the valuation conversation

Of the ten names we have initiated, Oracle is the one I am most confident explaining in a single sentence: the market is pricing it as a software company with uncertain AI exposure when it is actually a cloud infrastructure company with $553B in remaining performance obligations — contracted revenue that does not require an economic recovery, a Hormuz resolution, or a rate cut to materialise. At ~22× forward earnings against a 12-month average of ~44×, the discount is not subtle. Full thesis publishing this week.

Our positioning

We are not in cash. The data on market timing is unambiguous: the ten best single days for the S&P 500 since 1980 occurred largely during or immediately after the worst crisis environments — COVID, GFC, the dotcom crash. Missing those days while in cash is the surest path to long-run underperformance.17

We have initiated positions in ten names we believe are historically mispriced given the current environment. All trade at or below their 10-year historical mean P/E. All have contracted or structurally recurring revenue — the kind that does not require a Hormuz resolution to hold. We will publish the complete thesis for each over the coming weeks.

What to watch — catalyst calendar

The view from here

The assets we are buying are priced as if the current environment is permanent. It is not. Every structural regime change in the history of modern markets — oil embargo, dot-com crash, global financial crisis, COVID — eventually resolved, and the companies with the strongest underlying fundamentals recovered first. The distinction between regime change and correction matters here: in a correction you wait for the all-clear. In a regime change you position through the uncertainty, because the all-clear and the recovery often arrive simultaneously, and waiting costs you the best days in the market.

I will be transparent about one thing: I do not know how long this regime persists. The Tuesday Hormuz deadline is a genuine binary — it could resolve or escalate, and I have assigned 25% to the bull scenario not because I am confident but because that is my honest probability given what Iran rejected this morning. The thesis is specific enough to be wrong and we will say so clearly if it is. Every position is on the record. We will update it as the facts change.
